questions.question: What is an earthquake's focus, or hypocenter?
choices: The surface location directly above the rupture origin
The farthest point reached by a wave
The instrument recording the earthquake
The location where rupture begins inside Earth

questions.question: What is an earthquake's epicenter?
choices: The surface point directly above its focus
The deepest part of Earth's core
The first seismic station to detect shaking
The end of every fault

questions.question: Which body waves generally arrive first at a station?
choices: S waves
Surface waves
P waves
Ocean tides

questions.question: Which body waves involve shear motion?
choices: P waves
Sound waves in water only
S waves
Electromagnetic waves

questions.question: What is a seismogram?
choices: A recorded trace of ground motion
A map of mineral hardness
A measurement of rainfall
A model of ocean salinity

questions.question: What does earthquake magnitude summarize?
choices: Damage to one particular building
Shaking intensity at one observation site
The event's focal depth only
The earthquake's overall size

questions.question: What does earthquake intensity describe?
choices: The earthquake's identical size at every location
Shaking and effects at a particular location
The age of the fault
The exact time of the next earthquake

questions.question: Why can rocks suddenly slip along a fault?
choices: Accumulated stress can overcome resistance to movement
Faults contain no friction
All rock melts before every earthquake
Gravity stops briefly at the fault

questions.question: Why do P waves usually arrive before S waves?
choices: They are emitted only after S waves stop
They travel faster through the same rock
They travel only through air
They contain no energy

questions.question: Why does the P–S arrival-time gap help estimate distance?
choices: The gap gives only the earthquake's age
Both waves always arrive simultaneously
Wave speed is unrelated to travel time
The slower S wave falls increasingly behind over longer paths

questions.question: Why are records from several stations needed to locate an epicenter well?
choices: One station gives every possible direction exactly
Magnitude determines the epicenter without wave data
Different distance estimates constrain a common location
All stations must be placed on the same fault

questions.question: Why can intensity vary for the same earthquake?
choices: Distance, ground conditions, and structures affect local shaking and damage
Magnitude changes to a different event at each town
Every site contains identical rocks
Intensity is determined only by the event's name

questions.question: Why can soft sediments worsen shaking relative to nearby firm ground?
choices: They absorb every seismic wave completely
They stop surface waves from forming
They can amplify particular ground motions
They always have zero density

questions.question: What is an aftershock?
choices: A warning that always occurs before a main earthquake
An earthquake following a larger event in the same general region
An ocean wave produced by wind
A sound unrelated to fault movement

questions.question: Why are precise short-term earthquake predictions difficult?
choices: Scientists cannot measure ground motion
Every fault moves on an identical schedule
Earthquakes have no physical causes
Fault systems are complex, and exact event timing is not reliably predictable

questions.question: Station A has a P–S gap of 10 s; station B has 30 s. With comparable paths and known wave speeds, which is generally closer?
choices: Station B
They must be equally distant
The gaps measure only magnitude
Station A

questions.question: A quake has one magnitude but different reported intensities across towns. Is this consistent?
choices: No; every location must have the same intensity
Yes; local effects can vary for one event
No; intensity measures only core temperature
Yes; each town creates a separate magnitude for the same event

questions.question: S waves are absent after a path would pass through the outer core. What does this support?
choices: The mantle is entirely liquid
The core contains no matter
The outer core is liquid
P waves cannot pass through liquids

questions.question: A magnitude increase of one unit corresponds to roughly how much more released seismic energy?
choices: About 32 times
About 2 times
About 10 times
About 1,000 times

questions.question: Why can an undersea earthquake generate a tsunami in some cases?
choices: Every earthquake heats the whole ocean to boiling
Sudden seafloor displacement moves a large volume of water
Earthquake sound creates ordinary wind waves
All undersea earthquakes produce equally large tsunamis
